text:
This section examines Experiments B, C,
and D — Scaling,

operator matching, and deception from
first principles. Keep two questions

separate: does changing the order change
the measured outcome, and

does the proposed search method beat a
matched alternative at

the same distinct-evaluation budget? Typed
landscapes:

Hamming/absolute-position,
Kendall/precedence, and adjacency/routing.

Operators: swap, insert, inversion,
scramble. Sizes: nin{6,8,10,12,14,16}.

Repeats: 15 seeds per cell. Censoring cap:
10,000 generations in

the final protocol. Matched results at
n=16: swap on Hamming,

mean 405 generations; insert on Kendall,
mean 396; inversion on

adjacency, mean 1,199. Scaling exponents
from the log: approximately 2.79,

2.98, and 3.44 for the matched cases,
consistent with the

expected cubic-log trend over the tested
range. Failure mode: mismatched

operators on plateau-rich landscapes could
censor completely; deceptive

landscapes censored most runs by n=8–10
even with apparently smooth

local structure. Visual: a 3×4 heat map of
operator versus

landscape, followed by scaling curves.
Censored cells must have a

distinct hatch, not a fabricated numeric
value. Now read evidence

panel T4-scaling. The axes, units, and
sample are stated on

screen. The sample represented here is 15
seeds. Raw observations

remain visible wherever the artifact
provides them. Censored observations

stay marked at the cap rather than
becoming invented hitting

times, and sampled landscapes leave
unobserved permutations blank. The

supported finding is: Matched results at
n=16: swap on Hamming,

mean 405 generations; insert on Kendall,
mean 396; inversion on

adjacency, mean 1,199. The broader claim
not established here is:

The conclusion is scoped to the recorded
evaluator, landscape, and

budget. This evidence changed the program
as follows: Carry this

constraint into the next experiment and
compare methods at equal

cost. The distinction is part of the
result. A large

ordering effect does not automatically
imply an evolutionary-search

advantage, and almost-sure convergence
does not promise practical
efficiency.
